name: The Capitol Park Moon Tree

location.address: North side of the California State Capitol, beside the northeast security pavilion, 10th and L Streets, Sacramento

verified_sources: https://capitolmuseum.ca.gov/images/pdf/CapitolParkTreeBooklet.pdf (via web.archive.org, State Capitol Museum Capitol Park Tree Guide, updated 2016-09-01, p.8)
access: Free. Capitol Park is open to the public daily; the tree stands on the lawn at the north-east corner of the Capitol, by the security pavilion. Capitol Annex construction is under way nearby, so some paths may be fenced.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 37 metres on a crown only 12 metres across. It stands on the lawn at the Capitol's north-east corner, beside the security pavilion and behind the Sisters of Mercy sculpture.
transport: On foot in downtown Sacramento, at 10th and L Streets; bus and light rail routes not checked.
story:
This redwood went around the moon as a seed. In 1971 the command module pilot of Apollo 14 carried tree seeds supplied by the US Forest Service, and this one had been collected near Soquel in California in 1966.

The seedling was shipped from the Institute of Forest Genetics in Placerville on 2 April 1976 and planted that month in Capitol Park, about two feet tall. NASA's page gives the date as April 20, with a question mark, which is an honest thing to find on a NASA page. By NASA's 2024 update it was about 120 feet tall with a canopy of about 40.

It is Sacramento's only Moon Tree and one of seven in California. At fifty it is an infant by redwood standards, and the seed's journey is the reason to come.

The last few years have been nervy. The Capitol Annex project put dozens of the park's trees at risk, by official estimates 20 to 30 and by advocates' as many as 100. A 2023 news report said this one was protected in place, and NASA says the annex plans were designed to keep it safe. Our evidence that it still stands runs to 2024. If you visit, tell us.

name: The Deodars of the Capitol's West Front

location.address: West side of the California State Capitol, 10th Street between L and N, Sacramento

verified_sources: https://capitolmuseum.ca.gov/images/pdf/CapitolParkTreeBooklet.pdf (via web.archive.org, State Capitol Museum Capitol Park Tree Guide, updated 2016-09-01, pp.3, 6, 7)
https://annex.assembly.ca.gov/sites/annex.assembly.ca.gov/files/Capitol%20Tree%20Map.pdf (adapted from California State Parks Capitol Park Tree Listing, 2016-01-14)

official_register.name: California State Capitol Museum, Capitol Park Tree Guide

access: Free. Capitol Park is open to the public; the cedars line the lawn at the west entrance of the Capitol.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the number, ten tall cedars with drooping branches in one line. They stand on the lawn in front of the Capitol's west entrance.
transport: On foot in downtown Sacramento, along 10th Street between L and N; bus and light rail routes not checked.
story:
Somewhere in this row of ten stands the largest deodar in California, and the Capitol's own tree guide does not say which one. The State Capitol Museum's guide of 2016 gives the title to one of them, drawing on the California Big Trees Registry, and leaves you to work out the rest.

The guide also says that several of the ten belong to the Capitol's original twelve, planted in 1872. It does not say which several. That makes these trees, or some of them, more than 150 years old. Deodars are Himalayan cedars, a long way from home on a lawn in California's capital.

The row has had one recent scare. The Capitol Annex project put dozens of the park's trees at risk, 20 to 30 by the state's own estimate, though we have found no report of a cedar being removed. Someone photographed a deodar near the champion's registered position in October 2026, which suggests the row is intact without proving it.

For now they are best taken as a set, on the lawn at the west entrance. If you can tell us which is the champion, we would like to know.
